questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A 26-year-old washes her hands 60 times a day because of intrusive thoughts of contamination that she recognises as her own and senseless. Which combination is first-line treatment?
options: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a higher dose than for depression, with exposure and response prevention
A low-dose antipsychotic with supportive therapy
A benzodiazepine with relaxation training
Lithium with psychoeducation
questions.concept: The obsessions are recognised as the patient own and are resisted, which distinguishes them from delusions, and clomipramine is the alternative where a serotonin reuptake inhibitor fails.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Which feature is required for a diagnosis of generalised anxiety disorder?
options: Excessive free-floating worry about several domains, present on most days for at least 6 months, with autonomic and muscle tension symptoms
Discrete attacks of terror lasting minutes
Fear restricted to a single object
Anxiety only in social situations
questions.concept: The absence of a specific trigger is what makes the anxiety free-floating, and treatment combines a serotonergic antidepressant with cognitive behaviour therapy rather than long-term benzodiazepines.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A young man avoids meetings and eating in public because he fears being scrutinised and humiliated, and blushes and trembles when observed. What is the diagnosis?
options: Social anxiety disorder
Agoraphobia
Panic disorder
Schizoid personality disorder
questions.concept: The fear is of the judgement of others rather than of the situation itself, and a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor with cognitive behaviour therapy is preferred, with a beta blocker useful only for discrete performance anxiety.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Two months after surviving a bus accident a man has intrusive re-experiencing, nightmares, avoidance of travel and hypervigilance. What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
options: Post-traumatic stress disorder, treated with trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy and a serotonergic antidepressant
Acute stress reaction, treated with a benzodiazepine
Adjustment disorder, treated with reassurance alone
Dissociative amnesia, treated with hypnosis
questions.concept: An acute stress reaction resolves within days and adjustment disorder lacks the re-experiencing, and routine benzodiazepines are avoided because they impair the emotional processing that recovery depends on.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A woman has become unable to leave home alone, use buses or enter crowded markets for fear of being unable to escape if she becomes unwell. What is the diagnosis?
options: Agoraphobia, frequently with panic attacks
Social anxiety disorder
Specific phobia
Generalised anxiety disorder
questions.concept: The core fear is of being trapped without escape or help rather than of the crowd itself, and graded exposure with an antidepressant is effective while avoidance maintains and worsens the disorder.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A patient on alprazolam for 8 months needs increasing doses and becomes tremulous and anxious when a dose is missed. How should this be managed and what is the role of flumazenil?
options: Substitute a long-acting benzodiazepine such as diazepam and taper it slowly; flumazenil is reserved for acute overdose and may precipitate seizures in a dependent patient
Stop the drug abruptly and give flumazenil
Increase the dose indefinitely
Give flumazenil daily during the taper
questions.concept: Abrupt withdrawal risks seizures and a confusional state, and the antagonist is dangerous in dependence for the same reason, so the emphasis is on a gradual taper with psychological support.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Which drugs are used for opioid substitution treatment, and what is the rationale?
options: Buprenorphine or methadone, because a long-acting agonist prevents withdrawal and craving and reduces injecting risk
Naltrexone during acute withdrawal
Naloxone as maintenance
Disulfiram as maintenance
questions.concept: Naltrexone is used for relapse prevention only after detoxification is complete, because giving an antagonist to a dependent patient precipitates severe withdrawal.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: How does disulfiram help maintain abstinence from alcohol, and what must the patient be warned about?
options: It inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase so acetaldehyde accumulates and any alcohol causes flushing, vomiting and hypotension; hidden alcohol in medicines and mouthwash must be avoided
It reduces craving by blocking opioid receptors
It blocks alcohol absorption
It sedates the patient so drinking is unattractive
questions.concept: It works by deterrence rather than by altering craving, so it requires a motivated patient and supervision, and it is contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease and severe liver disease.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Which two drugs reduce craving rather than acting as a deterrent in alcohol dependence, and how do they differ?
options: Acamprosate, which modulates glutamate and is safe in liver disease, and naltrexone, an opioid antagonist that reduces the reward of drinking but is avoided in hepatic impairment
Disulfiram and thiamine
Diazepam and lorazepam
Baclofen and haloperidol
questions.concept: Either can be combined with psychosocial treatment, and the choice usually rests on liver function and on whether the patient is also using opioids, in which case the antagonist is contraindicated.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Which brief instrument is used to screen for hazardous and harmful alcohol use in a general clinic?
options: The AUDIT questionnaire, with the CAGE questions as a shorter alternative
The Mini-Mental State Examination
The Hamilton Depression Rating Scale
The Glasgow Coma Scale
questions.concept: Screening matters because most hazardous drinkers are not dependent and respond to brief advice, and biochemical markers such as gamma-glutamyl transferase and mean corpuscular volume support but do not replace the questionnaire.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Neurotic and Substance Use Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Which class of drug is first-line for moderate depression, and what happens if it is stopped abruptly?
options: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, and abrupt cessation can cause a discontinuation syndrome with dizziness, paraesthesiae, irritability and flu-like symptoms
A tricyclic antidepressant, with no withdrawal effects
A monoamine oxidase inhibitor, with no withdrawal effects
A benzodiazepine, which should be stopped abruptly
questions.concept: Paroxetine and venlafaxine with their short half-lives cause the syndrome most readily and fluoxetine least, so tapering over weeks is advised rather than stopping in one step.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A patient on an SSRI is given tramadol and develops agitation, hyperreflexia, clonus, diarrhoea and fever within hours. How does this differ from neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
options: Serotonin syndrome has a rapid onset with clonus, hyperreflexia and diarrhoea, whereas neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and marked creatine kinase elevation
Both present identically
Serotonin syndrome develops over weeks
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome features clonus
questions.concept: Treatment is withdrawal of the serotonergic drugs with supportive care and cyclohepatadine, while the neuroleptic syndrome needs dantrolene or bromocriptine, so the distinction changes management.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A woman is tearful and labile on the fourth day after delivery but functioning normally, resolving in a few days. How does this differ from postnatal depression and puerperal psychosis?
options: It is postpartum blues, which is common and self-limiting, whereas postnatal depression lasts weeks with functional impairment and puerperal psychosis presents early with delusions and disorganisation as a psychiatric emergency
All three are the same condition of differing severity requiring admission
Blues requires antidepressants
Psychosis appears only after 6 months
questions.concept: Puerperal psychosis carries a real risk of infanticide and suicide so it requires urgent admission, whereas the blues needs only support and observation.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A man has felt low in mood most of the time for 3 years without ever meeting criteria for a major depressive episode. What is the diagnosis?
options: Persistent depressive disorder, formerly dysthymia
Major depressive disorder in partial remission
Cyclothymia
Adjustment disorder
questions.concept: It responds to antidepressants and psychotherapy despite the chronic course, and a superimposed major episode is called double depression, which is why the chronic baseline is easily overlooked.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Which factors most strongly increase the immediate risk of suicide in a depressed patient?
options: A specific plan with available means, previous attempt, hopelessness, recent loss, and comorbid alcohol use
Female sex and young age alone
Presence of anxiety symptoms only
Mild sleep disturbance
questions.concept: Direct enquiry about suicidal intent does not increase risk and is essential, and a period of apparent improvement in energy before mood recovers is a recognised high-risk window.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A patient treated with an antidepressant for depression becomes elated, overtalkative and sleepless within 3 weeks. What has happened and how should treatment change?
options: An antidepressant-induced switch to mania, so the antidepressant is withdrawn and a mood stabiliser or antipsychotic started
Serotonin syndrome, so a benzodiazepine is added
Discontinuation syndrome, so the dose is increased
Akathisia, so a beta blocker is added
questions.concept: The episode reclassifies the illness as bipolar, so monotherapy with an antidepressant is thereafter avoided and future depressive episodes are treated under the cover of a mood stabiliser.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Which treatment is specific for depression that recurs each winter with hypersomnia, increased appetite and carbohydrate craving?
options: Bright light therapy, alongside standard antidepressant treatment
Electroconvulsive therapy as first line
Lithium monotherapy
Thyroxine
questions.concept: The reversed pattern of increased sleep and appetite is characteristic of this atypical presentation, and timing the light exposure to the morning is what makes the treatment effective.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: For how long should an antidepressant be continued after a first episode of depression has remitted, and why?
options: For at least 6 to 9 months at the effective dose, because stopping earlier substantially increases the risk of relapse
Stopped as soon as mood improves
Continued lifelong after a first episode
Halved as soon as symptoms improve
questions.concept: Recurrent episodes justify longer or indefinite treatment, and the commonest reason for apparent treatment failure is an inadequate dose or duration rather than a wrong drug.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Why is sodium valproate avoided as a mood stabiliser in a woman of childbearing potential?
options: It carries a high risk of neural tube defects and of impaired neurodevelopment in the child, so it is used only when alternatives have failed and effective contraception is in place
It causes infertility
It has no effect in bipolar disorder in women
It interacts with all contraceptives
questions.concept: Lithium carries a smaller and more specific cardiac risk while lamotrigine is comparatively safer, so the choice of stabiliser in a young woman is made with pregnancy in view from the outset.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: Why must a patient taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor avoid cheese, red wine and fermented foods?
options: Dietary tyramine is normally degraded by intestinal monoamine oxidase, and when the enzyme is inhibited it releases stored noradrenaline and causes a hypertensive crisis
These foods inactivate the drug
These foods cause serotonin syndrome
These foods block drug absorption
questions.concept: The crisis presents with severe headache and hypertension and is treated with phentolamine, and the same class must not be combined with a serotonergic drug without an adequate washout.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Mood Disorders

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Psychiatric history, mental status examination & classification (ICD/DSM)
questions.stem: How does circumstantiality differ from tangentiality in a patient speech?
options: In circumstantiality the patient eventually reaches the point after excessive irrelevant detail, whereas in tangentiality the reply veers away and never arrives at the point
Both never reach the point
Circumstantiality never reaches the point
Tangentiality involves invented words
questions.concept: Both are disorders of the form of thought rather than of content, and grading them from circumstantiality through tangentiality to loosening of associations and word salad reflects increasing severity.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Psychiatric History and Examination

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Psychiatric history, mental status examination & classification (ICD/DSM)
questions.stem: How does perseveration differ from stereotypy?
options: Perseveration is the inappropriate repetition of a previous response to a new stimulus, whereas stereotypy is a repetitive purposeless movement or phrase unrelated to any stimulus
Both are responses to new stimuli
Perseveration is purposeless and unprompted
Stereotypy is a repeated answer to questions
questions.concept: Perseveration points particularly to frontal lobe dysfunction and organic states, whereas stereotypy is seen in catatonia, autism and intellectual disability.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Psychiatric History and Examination

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Psychiatric history, mental status examination & classification (ICD/DSM)
questions.stem: What are echolalia and echopraxia?
options: Echolalia is senseless repetition of the examiner words and echopraxia is imitation of the examiner movements
Echolalia is repetition of one own words and echopraxia is refusal to move
Both refer to speech phenomena
Both refer to movement phenomena
questions.concept: They belong to the catatonic syndrome along with automatic obedience, negativism and waxy flexibility, and their presence should prompt a search for an organic cause as well as a psychiatric one.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Psychiatric History and Examination

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Psychiatric history, mental status examination & classification (ICD/DSM)
questions.stem: How does depersonalisation differ from derealisation?
options: In depersonalisation the patient feels detached or unreal in themselves, whereas in derealisation the surroundings feel unreal or dreamlike
Both refer to the surroundings
Depersonalisation refers to the surroundings
Derealisation refers to the body
questions.concept: Insight is retained in both, which distinguishes them from psychosis, and they occur in anxiety, dissociation, temporal lobe epilepsy and drug intoxication.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Psychiatric History and Examination

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Psychiatric history, mental status examination & classification (ICD/DSM)
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes an obsession from a compulsion?
options: An obsession is a recurrent intrusive thought, image or impulse, whereas a compulsion is the repetitive act or mental ritual performed to relieve it
An obsession is an act and a compulsion is a thought
Both are motor acts
Both are experienced as coming from outside
questions.concept: Both are recognised as the patient own and are resisted, and the sense of being one own thought is what separates an obsession from thought insertion in schizophrenia.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Psychiatric History and Examination

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Psychiatric history, mental status examination & classification (ICD/DSM)
questions.stem: What is an overvalued idea and how does it differ from a delusion?
options: It is an unreasonable belief pursued beyond the bounds of reason but which the person will concede is possibly wrong, whereas a delusion is held with unshakeable conviction
It is held with absolute conviction
It is always bizarre in content
It is a form of hallucination
questions.concept: The distinction is one of the degree of conviction rather than of content, and overvalued ideas are typical of anorexia nervosa, dysmorphophobia and hypochondriasis.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Psychiatric History and Examination

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Psychiatric history, mental status examination & classification (ICD/DSM)
questions.stem: What is a pseudohallucination?
options: A vivid perception experienced in inner subjective space and recognised as not real, unlike a true hallucination which is perceived in external space as real
A hallucination that occurs only at night
A misinterpretation of a real stimulus
A deliberately feigned hallucination
questions.concept: Grief reactions and dissociative states commonly produce them, so their recognition prevents a bereaved person being wrongly labelled psychotic.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Psychiatric History and Examination

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.topic: Psychiatric history, mental status examination & classification (ICD/DSM)
questions.stem: How does flight of ideas differ from clang association?
options: In flight of ideas the thoughts follow one another rapidly with understandable connections, whereas clang association links words by sound rather than by meaning
Both link words by sound
Flight of ideas has no discernible connection between thoughts
Clang association is a disorder of thought content
questions.concept: Flight of ideas with pressure of speech is characteristic of mania, whereas rhyming and punning links suggest a more severe disorganisation of thought form.
questions.reference: Ahuja A Short Textbook of Psychiatry 8e, Ch. Psychiatric History and Examination
